xrefs.title: Stretching out the hand

passages.en: And stretching out the hand (καὶ ἐκτείνας τὴν χεῖρα), he touched him, saying, “I want. Be clean.” And immediately his skin disease was made clean.

passages.ref: Exodus 3:20 (LXX, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible)
passages.en: and I will stretch out my hand (Καὶ ἐκτείνας τὴν χεῖρα lit. stretching out the hand), and smite the Egyptians with all my wonders, which I shall work among them, and after that he will send you forth.

xrefs.note: The same four Greek words. In Exodus the outstretched hand strikes Egypt with wonders; here it touches an outcast and makes him clean, the first of the wonders in Matthew 8–9.

xrefs.title: “Master”

passages.en: And look, a skin-diseased man, approaching, was bowing down to him, saying, “Master (Κύριε), if you want (θέλῃς), you are able to make me clean.”
Not everyone who says to me, “Master, master! (Κύριε κύριε)” will enter into the kingdom of the skies, but rather the one who does the desire (θέλημα) of my Father in the skies.

xrefs.note: The Sermon ends by warning that saying “Master” is not enough; what counts is the Father's desire. The first person down the mountain says “Master” and leaves it to Jesus' desire: “if you want” (θέλω, the root of θέλημα).

xrefs.title: “I am not worthy”

passages.en: And responding, the centurion said, “Master, I am not worthy (οὐκ εἰμὶ ἱκανὸς) that you come in under my roof, but only speak with a word, and my boy will be healed.

For I immerse y’all in water for a change-of-direction, but the one coming after me is more strong than me, whose sandal I am not worthy (οὐκ εἰμὶ ἱκανὸς) to carry. He will immerse you with the holy spirit and fire,

xrefs.note: Only two people in Matthew say these words: John the Baptist, about the one coming after him, and a Gentile centurion, about Jesus coming under his roof.

xrefs.title: Paralyzed, thrown down

passages.en: and saying, “Master, my boy has been thrown down (βέβληται) in the house, paralyzed (παραλυτικός), terribly tormented.”

Just then some men brought to Him a paralytic (παραλυτικὸν) lying (βεβλημένον lit. thrown down) on a mat. When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.”
passages.sources: Berean Standard Bible (public domain) · Greek: SBLGNT

passages.en: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority (ἐξουσίαν) on earth to forgive sins...” Then He said to the paralytic, “Get up, pick up your mat, and go home (ὕπαγε εἰς τὸν οἶκόν σου).”
passages.sources: Berean Standard Bible (public domain) · Greek: SBLGNT

xrefs.note: The same two words for a man who can't move: paralyzed, and thrown down (the same perfect tense of βάλλω). Both stories also turn on authority (8:9) and trust (8:10), and end with “Go” (8:13).

xrefs.title: Healed from a distance

passages.en: And responding, the centurion said, “Master, I am not worthy that you come in under my roof, but only speak with a word, and my boy will be healed (ἰαθήσεται).
“O woman,” Jesus answered, “your faith is great! Let it be done for you as you desire.” And her daughter was healed (ἰάθη) from that very hour.
passages.sources: Berean Standard Bible (public domain) · Greek: SBLGNT

xrefs.note: Matthew's stories use this healing word (ἰάομαι) for only two people: a Gentile centurion's boy / servant and a Canaanite woman's daughter, both healed from a distance after Jesus praises a Gentile's trust. (It appears once more, in a quote of Isaiah, 13:15.)
